title: A Skill-Swap Afternoon
description: Trade twenty minutes of something you can do for twenty minutes of something a friend can do. Both of you leave knowing more than you arrived with — and it costs nothing.

body.heading: How it works
paragraphs: Find one person who knows something you would like to learn — mending a hem, pruning a rose, playing three chords, folding a fitted sheet, cooking one good curry. Offer something you can show them in return. Agree a time, a place, and one small, specific thing each of you will teach.

Each teacher gets twenty minutes. The learner does the doing, not just the watching: hands on the guitar, hands in the dough. The teacher explains each step out loud as it happens, which is exactly what makes teaching such a powerful way to learn — the teacher has to organise what they know, and the gaps show up fast.

body.heading: Make the swap kind
paragraphs: Keep the goal tiny. One dish, one song, one seam — not a whole cuisine or instrument. End each turn by swapping one honest note: what worked, and what to practise next. Then swap roles and do it again.

If it goes well, make it a monthly habit and invite someone new each time. A neighbourhood where people trade skills is a neighbourhood where everyone keeps growing, and the price of a lesson is simply the willingness to share one.

takeaway: Everyone knows something worth teaching — and teaching it is how you learn it twice.
materials: A notebook and pen for each person
Whatever everyday tools the chosen skills need, for example a guitar, a mixing bowl, or a needle and thread
A quiet table and two chairs
supervision: Both swappers agree the time, place, and skill in advance; meet in a public or familiar place, and tell someone where you will be.
safetyNotes: Meet somewhere public or familiar for a first swap
Agree what tools are needed before you meet, so nothing is improvised on the spot
Use tools you already know how to handle safely, and show the learner the safe way first
